Similar cycle or reconstruction ideas powered unsupervised summarization, sentence compression,and opinion summarization (Wang and LEE, 202O; Baziotis et al., 2019; Brazinskas et al., 202O), as well as large-scale pseudo-pretraining from news leads (Yang et al., 2O2O). Cycle consistency was later applied to data-to-text generation (Guo et al., 2O2O). Because no gold validation exists, these studies chose checkpoints with roundtrip BLEU, reconstruction loss,or discriminator scores,which correlate well with true quality. We follow the same principle, using IR-to-document reconstruction to guide model selection forLLMscale training.

with pseudo-fine-tuning.

Paired by the Teacher (PbT) is a unified teacher-student pipeline that converts unpaired inputs and outputs into high-fidelity source-target pairs without any human labeling.

PbT Overview Figure 2 provides a high-level illustration of the PbT pipeline. The process unfolds in three phases. In the Source IR Induction phase, the teacher LLM compresses each unpaired source into a concise intermediate representation (IR),and the student model is trained to reconstruct the original input from this IR.In the Target IR Annotation phase, the teacher annotates each unpaired target with a plausible IR,which the trained student then expands into a synthetic source, forming paired examples $( \tilde { x } , y )$ . Finally, in the Downstream Fine-tuning phase,a summarization or questiongeneration model is fine-tuned on these synthetic pairs.By shifting heavy generation to the student while keeping the teacher's guidance at the IR level, PbT achieves both effciency and alignment (see Appendix A.3 for concrete IR examples).

We train the PbT model with the dialogues from SwitchBoard and summaries from DialogSum, aiming to train a summarization model that can summarize the dialogues from SwitchBoard into DialogSum-style summaries. Yen-Ju Lu, Thomas Thebaud, Laureano Moro-Velazquez, Najim Dehak, Jesus Villalba

# Abstract

We present Paired by the Teacher (PbT),a twostage teacher-student pipeline that synthesizes accurate input-output pairs without human labels or parallel data. In many low-resource natural language generation (NLG) scenarios, practitioners may have only raw outputs,like highlights,recaps,or questions, or only raw inputs, such as articles, dialogues, or paragraphs, but seldom both. This mismatch forces small models to learn from very few examples or rely on costly, broad-scope synthetic examples produced by large LLMs. PbT addresses this by asking a teacher LLM to compress each unpaired example into a concise intermediate representation (IR),and training a student to reconstruct inputs from IRs.This enables outputs to be paired with student-generated inputs, yielding high-quality synthetic data. We evaluate PbT on five benchmarks-document summarization (XSum, CNNDM), dialogue summarization (SAMSum,DialogSum),and question generation (SQuAD)—as well as an unpaired setting on SwitchBoard (paired with DialogSum summaries).An 8B student trained only on PbT data outperforms models trained on 70 B teacher-generated corpora and other unsupervised baselines,coming within 1.2 ROUGEL of human-annotated pairs and closing $82 \%$ of the oracle gap at one-third the annotation cost of direct synthesis.Human evaluation on SwitchBoard further confirms that only PbT produces concise,faithful summaries aligned with the target style, highlighting its advantage of generating in-domain sources that avoid the mismatch,limiting direct synthesis.

Many NLG tasks, such as summarization and question generation, lack readily available input-output pairs,often referred to as source-target pairs. It also raises privacy concerns when conversations contain sensitive information. To solve this problem, we introduce Paired by the Teacher (PbT). Given only unpaired in-domain texts and a small set of example summaries or questions, PbT generates high-quality synthetic source-target pairs without any human pairing. This pipeline turns raw data into ready training material that matches the target style and speeds up adaptation across domains.

In the Source IR Induction phase, the teacher LLM compresses each unpaired source into a concise intermediate representation (IR),and the student model is trained to reconstruct the original input from this IR.In the Target IR Annotation phase, the teacher annotates each unpaired target with a plausible IR,which the trained student then expands into a synthetic source, forming paired examples $( \tilde { x } , y )$ . Finally, in the Downstream Fine-tuning phase,a summarization or questiongeneration model is fine-tuned on these synthetic pairs.By shifting heavy generation to the student while keeping the teacher's guidance at the IR level, PbT achieves both effciency and alignment (see Appendix A.3 for concrete IR examples).

# 3.1Source-side IR Learning

Our pipeline begins by teaching the student model to reconstruct in-domain source data from the IR. We first use a large teacher model $\tau$ to extract a structured IR from each raw source example, and then fine-tune a smaller student model $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ to invert that mapping.

IR Extraction (Teacher） As illustrated in Figure 3a, for every unpaired source instance $x$ (dialogue,article, paragraph,..), the teacher $\tau$ produces a concise IR $m _ { x }$ (e.g.,a topical outline, chain-of-thought, or related facts). This yields a semi-supervised dataset of $( x _ { i } , m _ { x _ { i } } )$ pairs:

$$
\{ ( x _ { i } , m _ { x _ { i } } ) \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } .
$$

The form of $m _ { x _ { i } }$ is task-dependent. For dialogue and document summarization, the teacher is instructed to split the input into paragraph groups and write a topic sentence with key entities. For question generation, the teacher extracts the answercontaining sentence and writes supporting facts as bullets.These task-specific IRs provide the information needed to reconstruct the source $x _ { i }$ (see Table 12).

IR-to-Source Induction (Student） We then finetune the student model $s$ with parameter-efficient methods (PEFT) on these source-side annotations to learn the inverse mapping

$$
S _ { m  x } : m \mapsto x .
$$

By optimizing on $( x _ { i } , m _ { x _ { i } } )$ , the student internalizes the source domain's structural patterns and can expand IRs into realistic source texts $\hat { x } = S _ { \theta } ( m )$ The model is trained with the reconstruction loss

$$
\theta = \arg \operatorname* { m i n } _ { \theta } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } \mathcal { L } _ { R } ( S _ { \theta } ( m _ { x _ { i } } ) , x _ { i } ) ,
$$

where $\mathcal { L } _ { R }$ is the cross-entropy loss. These learned synthesis skills later allow $s$ to generate candidate sources for unpaired targets.

# 3.2Target-side IR Annotation

IR Annotation (Teacher)As shown in Figure 3b, we prompt the teacher LLM $\tau$ to annotate each unpaired target example $y$ with a plausible IR $\tilde { m } _ { y }$ To ensure consistent formatting, $\tau$ is provided with a few in-context examples of $( x , m _ { x } )$ pairs from the source-side training phase. This yields a set of target annotations:

$$
\{ ( y _ { j } , \tilde { m } _ { y _ { j } } ) \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { N _ { y } } .
$$

Because the teacher does not observe the corresponding source $x _ { j }$ , the generated $\tilde { m } _ { y _ { j } }$ are not aligned with the actual sources. Such explicit alignment is unnecessary, as the student generates synthetic sources directly from these IRs.

IR-to-Source Generation (Student) Once the student model $\cal { S } _ { m \to x }$ has learned to expand IRs into full source texts, we apply it to each target-side representation $\tilde { m } _ { y _ { j } }$ . The student then produces a synthetic source $\tilde { x } _ { j }$ for each target $y _ { j }$ , resulting in a synthetic paired corpus

$$
\{ ( \tilde { x } _ { j } , y _ { j } ) \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { N _ { y } } ,
$$

where every target is matched with a candidate source generated solely from its corresponding IR.

# 3.3Target Task Training

Finally, we fine-tune a downstream student model $S _ { x  y }$ on the synthetic pairs $\{ ( \tilde { x } _ { j } , y _ { j } ) \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { N _ { y } }$ The model learns to map synthetic sources to targets:

$$
S _ { x  y } : \tilde { x } \mapsto y .
$$

The training objective is

$$
\phi = \arg \operatorname* { m i n } _ { \phi } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { N _ { y } } \mathcal { L } _ { S } \big ( S _ { \phi } ( \tilde { x } _ { j } ) , y _ { j } \big ) ,
$$

yielding predictions $\hat { y } = S _ { \phi } ( \tilde { x } )$

PbT mimics the effect of having true training pairs for two reasons. First, it generates only synthetic source inputs $\tilde { x }$ and pairs them with authentic targets $y$ ， avoiding propagation of synthesis artifacts into outputs. Second, by training the student on real source data, PbT ensures that synthetic sources remain in-domain. As a result, at test time, PbT-generated pairs better match the distribution of real inputs,unlike direct synthesis,which suffers from mismatched sources.

# Limitations

While synthesizing data, we train the student to reconstruct the source text in an open-ended manner.PbT generally introduces fewer hallucinations than directly synthesizing from the target. However, because the IR inevitably omits some details, the generated sources and summaries still require careful human review in high-fidelity applications. All current experiments use English corpora only. We have not yet studied other languages or crosslingual scenarios such as summarizing documents or dialogues written in a different language.

# Ethical Considerations

As we extend the frontiers of NLP, we remain attentive to the ethical dimensions of our work. Generating synthetic data with large-scale models reduces our reliance on vast real-world datasets that could include personal or sensitive information. To uphold privacy and meet regulatory standards, we draw exclusively on openly available corpora under permissive terms (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and CC BY-NC-SA 4.O) and enforce stringent anonymization measures.When PbT is applied to copyrighted web or news material, the synthetic sources can echo portions of the originals.Practitioners should verify redistribution rights or ensure that outputs are sufficiently transformed. For conversational data, intermediate representations may reveal private entities or sensitive details,so names should be anonymized before teacher annotation. Finally, because PbT makes it easier to create large paired datasets, the same pipeline could be exploited to mass-produce malicious content. To limit misuse, we will release the code under a research-only license.
